name: Ensign
insignia_alt: Single gold bar — U.S. Navy Ensign collar device
meta_title: Ensign (ENS / O-1) — U.S. Navy Officer Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Ensign (ENS, O-1) — the Navy's entry-level commissioned officer rank for new division officers. Insignia, pay, history, career path, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's entry-grade commissioned officer — newly commissioned division officers and student aviators.
overview:
Ensign (ENS) is the most junior commissioned officer rank in the U.S. Navy, paygrade O-1, and the entry point for nearly every commissioning source — the U.S. Naval Academy, NROTC, Officer Candidate School (OCS), and direct commissions in restricted line and staff communities. New Ensigns typically report aboard ship or to flight school within months of commissioning and are expected to begin learning the practical art of leading Sailors in their first division-officer tour.

The rank insignia is a single gold bar worn on the collar or shoulder boards (one half-inch gold stripe on dress uniforms). Aboard ship, an Ensign is addressed verbally as "Mister" or "Miss" followed by their last name; in writing, the rank "Ensign" is spelled out. Ensigns are commissioned by the President of the United States and serve at the pleasure of the President under Title 10 of the U.S. Code.
history:
The rank of Ensign in the U.S. Navy was authorized in 1862, replacing the older grade of Passed Midshipman. The title is borrowed from the British military, where an "ensign" was historically the most junior commissioned officer assigned to carry the unit's colors — its ensign — into battle. In the modern Navy, the rank is the universal entry grade for newly commissioned officers from every accession source.

Ensigns commissioned through the U.S. Naval Academy and NROTC are obligated to serve a minimum active-duty service commitment that varies by community — typically five years for surface and submarine officers, eight or more years for aviators after winging. Most Ensigns who continue to perform satisfactorily promote to Lieutenant (Junior Grade) after approximately two years of commissioned service.
responsibilities: Serve as a Division Officer aboard ship, leading 10–40 enlisted Sailors
Stand watch as Officer of the Deck (Underway) qualified after qualification
Complete community-specific qualifications — Surface Warfare, Submarine, Aviation, etc.
Manage division training, maintenance, and administrative readiness
addressing: Verbally "Ensign Smith" or, informally aboard ship, "Mister/Miss Smith." In writing: "ENS Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: U.S. citizenship and accession via USNA, NROTC, OCS, or direct commission
Bachelor's degree (waivable for some staff-corps direct commissions)
Satisfactory completion of officer indoctrination/commissioning training
common_assignments: Division Officer aboard a surface combatant or amphibious ship
Student Naval Aviator or Student Naval Flight Officer at NAS Pensacola or NAS Whiting Field
Submarine Officer Basic Course student at Naval Submarine School, Groton, CT
Junior staff-corps officer (Supply, Civil Engineer Corps, Medical Service Corps)

pay_range.note: 2026 Defense Finance and Accounting Service basic pay table; excludes BAH, BAS, and special pays.

related_base_note: Many Ensigns are commissioned at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, MD.

faqs.question: How long does an Ensign typically serve before promotion?
faqs.answer: An Ensign typically serves about two years before promotion to Lieutenant (Junior Grade) (O-2). Promotion to O-2 is generally automatic for officers who remain in good standing and meet time-in-grade requirements.

faqs.question: What does an Ensign do aboard a Navy ship?
faqs.answer: A new Ensign aboard ship typically serves as a Division Officer, leading a small group of enlisted Sailors in a specialty area (e.g., Combat Information Center, Engineering, Deck) while qualifying as Officer of the Deck and pursuing warfare-pin qualifications.

faqs.question: How is an Ensign addressed?
faqs.answer: In conversation, an Ensign is addressed as "Ensign [Last Name]" or, informally aboard ship, as "Mister" or "Miss" followed by their last name. In writing, the abbreviation is ENS.

name: Lieutenant Junior Grade
insignia_alt: Single silver bar — U.S. Navy Lieutenant Junior Grade collar device
meta_title: Lieutenant Junior Grade (LTJG / O-2) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Lieutenant Junior Grade (LTJG) is the U.S. Navy O-2 commissioned officer rank. Learn the role, insignia, pay, addressing, and career path of a Navy LTJG.
h1: Lieutenant Junior Grade (LTJG) — U.S. Navy O-2
hero_tagline: The second commissioned officer rank — division officers earning their warfare pin.
overview:
Lieutenant Junior Grade (LTJG) is the second commissioned officer rank in the U.S. Navy at paygrade O-2. Most officers reach the grade approximately two years after commissioning as an Ensign and continue serving in the same division-officer billet aboard ship or as a winged aviator beginning fleet-replacement training.

The insignia is a single silver bar (the "butter bar" upgraded to silver), worn on collar devices and shoulder boards alongside one and a half stripes of gold lace on the sleeve of the service dress blue uniform. LTJGs typically continue to mature in their first sea tour, pursuing or completing warfare-pin qualifications such as the Surface Warfare Officer (SWO) pin, Naval Aviator wings, Naval Flight Officer wings, or Submarine Warfare insignia ("dolphins").
history:
The grade of Lieutenant Junior Grade was created by Congress in 1883, replacing the older title "Master." The intent was to provide a clear intermediate grade between the entry-level Ensign and the more senior Lieutenant — a structure largely shared with the U.S. Coast Guard and the U.S. Public Health Service Commissioned Corps. The Navy is the only U.S. military service that uses the title "Lieutenant Junior Grade" rather than "First Lieutenant" for its O-2 grade.

The promotion from Ensign to LTJG, like LTJG to Lieutenant, is generally a fully-qualified ("running mate") promotion: officers who remain in good standing typically pin on O-2 after roughly two years of commissioned service.
responsibilities: Continue Division Officer duties or transition to a more senior division
Complete warfare-pin qualification (SWO, Aviator, NFO, Submarine, EOD, SEAL, etc.)
Stand independent watches such as Officer of the Deck (Underway) or aircrew duties
Mentor newly reporting Ensigns and lead division training programs
addressing: Verbally "Lieutenant Smith" — both LTJG and full Lieutenant are addressed as "Lieutenant" in conversation. In writing: "LTJG Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Approximately two years of satisfactory commissioned service as an Ensign
Time-in-grade and time-in-service requirements per BUPERS instruction
common_assignments: Senior Division Officer aboard surface combatants and amphibious ships
Fleet Replacement Squadron student / first-tour aviator
Junior Officer assigned to a submarine department
Junior staff-corps officer in a fleet or shore billet

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table; excludes allowances and special pays.

related_base_note: Many LTJGs serve their first division-officer tours aboard ships homeported at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: How long does a Lieutenant Junior Grade serve before promotion?
faqs.answer: A LTJG typically serves about two years before promotion to Lieutenant (O-3). Promotion is generally automatic for officers in good standing who meet time-in-grade requirements.

faqs.question: How is the LTJG insignia different from a full Lieutenant?
faqs.answer: A LTJG wears a single silver bar; a Lieutenant wears two silver bars ("railroad tracks"). On the service dress blue uniform, an LTJG wears one full and one half stripe of gold lace; a Lieutenant wears two full stripes.

name: Lieutenant
insignia_alt: Two silver bars — U.S. Navy Lieutenant collar device
meta_title: Lieutenant (LT / O-3) — U.S. Navy Officer Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Lieutenant (LT, O-3) — the Navy's senior company-grade officer rank, equivalent to an Army Captain. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's senior company-grade officer — department heads-in-training and seasoned aviators.
overview:
Lieutenant (LT) is the U.S. Navy O-3 commissioned officer rank, equivalent to a Captain in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. It is widely considered the first "real" professional grade in the Navy: most officers wear two silver bars by the four-year point in their commissioned service, and many will spend the next four to six years completing a department-head sea tour or accumulating major aviation flight hours.

The insignia is two silver bars ("railroad tracks") worn on the collar or shoulder boards. On the service dress blue uniform, a Lieutenant wears two full stripes of gold lace on each sleeve. Lieutenants typically lead larger divisions, qualify and serve as Tactical Action Officer (TAO) or Engineering Officer of the Watch (EOOW), and often pin on warfare insignia or department-head qualification during this grade.
history:
The grade of Lieutenant has existed in the U.S. Navy since the Navy's founding in 1775. The title traces to the French "lieu tenant" — literally "place holder" — meaning an officer who held a position in the absence of a more senior commander. In the Royal Navy and early U.S. Navy, Lieutenants were the workhorse junior officers who stood watch on quarterdeck and commanded smaller vessels detached from the main fleet.

Promotion from LTJG to LT is the last "running mate" promotion in the modern Navy — most officers who remain in good standing pin on O-3 at approximately the four-year service mark. The next promotion, to Lieutenant Commander, is the first fully-competitive selection-board promotion in an officer's career.
responsibilities: Serve as Department Head (DH) on a smaller ship or as a senior Division Officer
Qualify and stand watch as Tactical Action Officer (TAO), EOOW, or Aircraft Mission Commander
Lead training, manning, and readiness for a major shipboard department
Begin building a record for the Lieutenant Commander selection board
addressing: Verbally "Lieutenant Smith." In writing: "LT Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Approximately four years of satisfactory commissioned service
Successful completion of warfare-pin qualification
Satisfactory fitness reports (FITREPs) at the LTJG grade
common_assignments: Department Head aboard a frigate, mine countermeasures ship, or PCU/precommissioning unit
Naval Aviator or NFO assigned to a fleet squadron
Submarine Officer in a department-head pipeline
Junior officer at a Type Commander or Numbered Fleet staff

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: Many Pacific Fleet Lieutenants serve department-head tours aboard ships homeported at Naval Base San Diego.

faqs.question: Is a Navy Lieutenant the same as an Army Captain?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Navy Lieutenant (O-3) is equivalent in paygrade and seniority to a Captain in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force.

faqs.question: When does a Lieutenant promote to Lieutenant Commander?
faqs.answer: Promotion from Lieutenant to Lieutenant Commander (O-4) is the first fully-competitive selection-board promotion in a Navy officer's career. It typically occurs at the 9–11 year service mark and is not automatic.

name: Lieutenant Commander
insignia_alt: Gold oak leaf — U.S. Navy Lieutenant Commander collar device
meta_title: Lieutenant Commander (LCDR / O-4) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Lieutenant Commander (LCDR, O-4) — the Navy's first field-grade rank and first selection-board promotion. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's first field-grade officer — department heads, executive officers of small commands, and seasoned staff officers.
overview:
Lieutenant Commander (LCDR) is the U.S. Navy O-4 commissioned officer rank, equivalent to a Major in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. It is the first field-grade rank and the first that requires selection by a statutory promotion board — typically at the 9–11 year service mark. The first selection-board promotion is a significant milestone in an officer's career, often determining whether they will continue toward the senior officer ranks.

LCDR insignia is a gold oak leaf, worn on the collar or shoulder boards. On the service dress blue uniform, a LCDR wears two full stripes plus one half stripe of gold lace. Lieutenant Commanders are typically expected to complete a department-head tour at sea, an executive-officer tour at a smaller command, or a major staff tour ashore.
history:
The grade of Lieutenant Commander was authorized by Congress in 1862 to fill a long-recognized gap between Lieutenant and Commander, mirroring the British Royal Navy. Before that point, the U.S. Navy promoted directly from Lieutenant to Commander, which made selection cycles less flexible and rotation between sea and shore more abrupt.

The promotion from Lieutenant to Lieutenant Commander is the first fully-competitive selection-board promotion in a Navy officer's career, with promotion opportunity historically running 70–85% for officers in the primary zone.
responsibilities: Department Head aboard a destroyer, cruiser, amphibious assault ship, or aircraft carrier
Executive Officer (XO) of a smaller command — submarine, MCM ship, expeditionary unit
Major staff officer at a Type Commander, Numbered Fleet, or Joint staff
Joint Professional Military Education (JPME) phase I attendance
addressing: Verbally "Commander Smith" — both LCDR and full Commander are addressed as "Commander." In writing: "LCDR Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by an O-4 statutory promotion board
Approximately 9–11 years of commissioned service
Strong fitness reports (FITREPs) at the Lieutenant grade
common_assignments: Department Head aboard a CG/DDG, amphibious ship, or aircraft carrier
XO of a submarine, mine countermeasures ship, or expeditionary squadron
Action officer on the OPNAV staff (Navy headquarters, Pentagon)
Aviation Department Head — Operations, Maintenance, or Training

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: Mayport-homeported destroyers and amphibious ships routinely embark LCDR-grade department heads.

faqs.question: Is the LCDR promotion automatic?
faqs.answer: No. Promotion to Lieutenant Commander is the first fully-competitive selection-board promotion in a Navy officer's career. Officers must be selected by an O-4 statutory promotion board.

faqs.question: What is the difference between LCDR and CDR?
faqs.answer: A LCDR (O-4) wears a gold oak leaf; a Commander (O-5) wears a silver oak leaf. Commanders are typically eligible for command of a major ship, squadron, or shore activity; LCDRs serve as department heads or executive officers of smaller commands.

name: Commander
insignia_alt: Silver oak leaf — U.S. Navy Commander collar device
meta_title: Commander (CDR / O-5) — U.S. Navy Officer Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Commander (CDR, O-5) — the Navy's field-grade rank eligible to command destroyers, submarines, and squadrons. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's O-5 field-grade officer — commanders of destroyers, submarines, and aviation squadrons.
overview:
Commander (CDR) is the U.S. Navy O-5 commissioned officer rank, equivalent to a Lieutenant Colonel in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. CDRs are eligible for command of a major surface combatant (destroyer, frigate), an attack or guided-missile submarine, an aviation squadron, or a significant shore command. Promotion to CDR is a statutory selection-board promotion and is one of the most significant milestones in a Navy officer's career.

CDR insignia is a silver oak leaf, worn on the collar or shoulder boards. On the service dress blue uniform, a Commander wears three full stripes of gold lace. Commander-select officers typically complete a major command pipeline — Prospective Commanding Officer (PCO) training, the Submarine Command Course, or aviation pre-command coursework.
history:
The rank of Commander has existed in the U.S. Navy since the early 19th century, originally referring to officers commanding sloops-of-war and other vessels too small to warrant a full Captain. The modern paygrade O-5 structure was set by the Officer Personnel Act of 1947, which standardized promotion zones and selection-board procedures across the Navy.

In the modern Navy, command at the O-5 level — particularly command of a destroyer or attack submarine — is widely viewed as the defining tour of a sea-going officer's career and is a statutory prerequisite for major-command (O-6) consideration.
responsibilities: Commanding Officer of a destroyer, frigate, MCM, attack submarine, or aviation squadron
Executive Officer of a deep-draft (cruiser, large amphibious ship) or aircraft carrier
Action officer or branch head at OPNAV, fleet, or Joint staffs
Senior staff officer at a Carrier Strike Group or Expeditionary Strike Group
addressing: Verbally "Commander Smith." In writing: "CDR Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by an O-5 statutory promotion board
Successful completion of an O-4 department-head, XO, or major-staff tour
Joint Professional Military Education (JPME) Phase I
common_assignments: CO of a guided-missile destroyer (DDG), submarine (SSN/SSGN), or fleet squadron
XO of a cruiser, amphibious assault ship, or aircraft carrier
Branch Head on the OPNAV or Joint Staff
Type Commander Surface, Submarine, or Aviation Force staff officer

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: Submarine Commanding Officers operating from Naval Base Kitsap typically hold the rank of Commander.

faqs.question: What ships can a Commander command?
faqs.answer: A Navy Commander (O-5) is typically eligible for command of a guided-missile destroyer (DDG), littoral combat ship (LCS), mine countermeasures ship (MCM), attack submarine (SSN), guided-missile submarine (SSGN), or an aviation squadron.

faqs.question: Is a Navy Commander the same as an Army Lieutenant Colonel?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Navy Commander (O-5) is equivalent in paygrade and seniority to a Lieutenant Colonel in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force.

name: Captain
insignia_alt: Silver eagle — U.S. Navy Captain collar device
meta_title: Captain (CAPT / O-6) — U.S. Navy Senior Officer Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Captain (CAPT, O-6) — the Navy's senior officer rank below flag, commanding carriers and cruisers. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's most senior officer rank below flag — commanders of carriers, cruisers, ballistic-missile submarines, and major shore commands.
overview:
Captain (CAPT) is the U.S. Navy O-6 commissioned officer rank, equivalent to a Colonel in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. The rank carries enormous prestige in the sea services because of the historical association with command of a ship: in the U.S. Navy, only the Commanding Officer of a vessel is referred to verbally as "Captain" regardless of their paygrade. A four-stripe Captain (O-6) is eligible for major sea command — an aircraft carrier, cruiser, ballistic-missile submarine, or a major shore installation.

CAPT insignia is a silver eagle ("scrambled eggs" begin appearing on the dress cap visor as well), worn on the collar or shoulder boards. On the service dress blue uniform, a Captain wears four full stripes of gold lace. Captains are eligible for selection to flag rank — promotion to Rear Admiral (Lower Half), O-7 — through a separate, highly competitive flag-officer selection board.
history:
The grade of Captain in the U.S. Navy dates to the founding of the Continental Navy in 1775. For more than a century, "Captain" was the most senior rank in the U.S. Navy — there were no Admirals in the U.S. Navy until 1862, when Congress authorized the rank of Rear Admiral specifically to honor David Glasgow Farragut for his service in the Civil War.

Today, command of a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier or a ballistic-missile submarine at the O-6 level is among the most demanding command tours in the U.S. military, typically following decades of operational, joint, and major-command experience.
responsibilities: Commanding Officer of an aircraft carrier (CVN), cruiser (CG), or ballistic-missile submarine (SSBN/SSGN)
Commanding Officer of a major shore installation or training command
Air Wing Commander (CAG) of a Carrier Air Wing
Major staff director at OPNAV, the Joint Staff, or a Combatant Command
addressing: Verbally "Captain Smith." In writing: "CAPT Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by an O-6 statutory promotion board
Successful completion of an O-5 major command or major staff tour
Joint Professional Military Education (JPME) Phase II for many billets
common_assignments: CO of an aircraft carrier (CVN), cruiser (CG), or SSBN
Commanding Officer of a major shore installation (e.g., NAS Pensacola, NAS Lemoore)
Carrier Air Wing Commander (CAG)
Director on the OPNAV, Joint Staff, or Combatant Command staff

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table; O-6 pay caps below the highest pay tier without 30+ years of service.

related_base_note: NAS Pensacola, the "Cradle of Naval Aviation," is commanded by a Navy Captain.

faqs.question: Is a Navy Captain the same as an Army Captain?
faqs.answer: No. A Navy Captain is paygrade O-6 — equivalent to an Army or Marine Corps Colonel. An Army Captain is paygrade O-3, equivalent to a Navy Lieutenant.

faqs.question: Why is a ship's Commanding Officer called "Captain"?
faqs.answer: In the U.S. Navy, the Commanding Officer of any commissioned vessel is referred to verbally as "Captain" regardless of their actual paygrade — even if the CO holds a junior rank such as Lieutenant. The title comes from the position, not the rank.

name: Rear Admiral (Lower Half)
insignia_alt: One silver star — U.S. Navy Rear Admiral (Lower Half) flag insignia
meta_title: Rear Admiral (Lower Half) (RDML / O-7) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Rear Admiral (Lower Half) (RDML, O-7) — the Navy's one-star flag officer rank. Insignia, pay, history, command opportunities, and how to address one.
h1: Rear Admiral (Lower Half) (RDML) — U.S. Navy O-7
hero_tagline: The Navy's one-star flag officer — destroyer squadron and carrier strike group deputies.
overview:
Rear Admiral (Lower Half) (RDML) is the U.S. Navy O-7 flag officer rank — the first general/flag-officer grade in the Navy. RDMLs wear one silver star and are equivalent in paygrade to a Brigadier General in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. The grade was distinguished from "upper half" Rear Admirals (O-8) by Congress in 1981 to bring U.S. Navy flag-officer pay in line with the rest of the Department of Defense.

Selection to flag rank is one of the most competitive promotions in the U.S. military — typically only a small fraction of eligible Captains are selected to RDML each year. RDMLs command at the strike-group, destroyer-squadron, and major-program level.
history:
Until the National Defense Authorization Act of 1981, the Navy used a single grade of "Commodore" or "Rear Admiral (Lower Half)" that was paid at the O-7 rate but wore the two stars of an O-8. The 1981 reform created today's clean structure: RDML (O-7, one star) and RADM (O-8, two stars). The Navy briefly resurrected "Commodore" as a one-star title in the 1980s before reverting to "Rear Admiral (Lower Half)."

Promotion to flag rank is governed by 10 U.S.C. and is subject to confirmation by the United States Senate.
responsibilities: Commander, Carrier Strike Group (CSG) or Expeditionary Strike Group (ESG) — typically two-star, but RDML deputies are common
Commander, Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) or Submarine Squadron (SUBRON)
Deputy Commander of a Numbered Fleet or Type Commander
Major program executive officer (PEO) at NAVSEA, NAVAIR, or SPAWAR/NAVWAR
addressing: Verbally "Admiral Smith" — all flag officers are addressed simply as "Admiral." In writing: "RDML Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by a flag-officer promotion board and confirmation by the U.S. Senate
Successful command at the O-6 level (major command at sea or ashore)
Joint Professional Military Education (JPME) Phase II
common_assignments: Commander, Destroyer Squadron (CDS / DESRON)
Deputy Commander of a Carrier Strike Group
Director of a major OPNAV resource sponsor (e.g., N96, N97, N98)
Program Executive Officer at NAVSEA or NAVAIR

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table; subject to statutory pay caps applicable to senior officers.

related_base_note: Many East Coast destroyer squadron commanders (RDMLs) are based at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: Why are there two grades of Rear Admiral?
faqs.answer: The Navy has historically used "Rear Admiral" for both one-star (O-7) and two-star (O-8) flag officers. Since 1981 they are statutorily distinct: Rear Admiral (Lower Half) is O-7 and wears one star; Rear Admiral is O-8 and wears two stars.

faqs.question: Is RDML equivalent to an Army Brigadier General?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Navy Rear Admiral (Lower Half) (O-7) is equivalent in paygrade and seniority to a Brigadier General in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force.

sources.label: 10 U.S.C. § 526 — Authorized strength: general and flag officers on active duty

name: Rear Admiral
insignia_alt: Two silver stars — U.S. Navy Rear Admiral flag insignia
meta_title: Rear Admiral (RADM / O-8) — U.S. Navy Two-Star Flag Officer | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Rear Admiral (RADM, O-8) — the Navy's two-star flag rank, commanding carrier and expeditionary strike groups. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's two-star flag officer — commanders of carrier strike groups and expeditionary strike groups.
overview:
Rear Admiral (RADM) is the U.S. Navy O-8 flag officer rank — a two-star admiral, equivalent in paygrade to a Major General in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. RADMs command Carrier Strike Groups (CSGs), Expeditionary Strike Groups (ESGs), Submarine Group commands, and major shore activities. Promotion from RDML (O-7) to RADM (O-8) is by selection board, confirmed by the U.S. Senate.

The two-star Rear Admiral is the most common operational flag-officer grade in the modern Navy and is the rank most often associated with at-sea strike-group command.
history:
The Navy created the rank of Rear Admiral in 1862 to recognize David Glasgow Farragut, the first U.S. Navy officer to hold flag rank. Until 1981, the Navy used a single "Rear Admiral" title for both one- and two-star paygrades. After the 1981 reform, "Rear Admiral" was reserved for O-8 (two stars) and "Rear Admiral (Lower Half)" was created for O-7 (one star).

The "rear" in the title is historical: in age-of-sail squadron formations, the Rear Admiral commanded the rearmost division of a fleet, the Vice Admiral the center, and the Admiral the van.
responsibilities: Commander, Carrier Strike Group (CSG) — embarked aboard a nuclear aircraft carrier
Commander, Expeditionary Strike Group (ESG)
Commander, Submarine Group
Director of a major Navy shore activity, training command, or laboratory
addressing: Verbally "Admiral Smith." In writing: "RADM Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by a flag-officer promotion board and Senate confirmation
Successful service at the O-7 grade in command or major staff billets
common_assignments: Commander, Carrier Strike Group (CSG-1 through CSG-12)
Commander, Expeditionary Strike Group (ESG-2, ESG-3, ESG-7)
Deputy Commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet or U.S. Fleet Forces Command
Director, OPNAV branch or warfighting division

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table; subject to statutory pay cap.

related_base_note: Atlantic Fleet Carrier Strike Group commanders (RADMs) are based at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: What does a Carrier Strike Group commander do?
faqs.answer: A Carrier Strike Group commander — typically a Rear Admiral (O-8) — commands a deployable strike group consisting of an aircraft carrier, its embarked Carrier Air Wing, and a destroyer squadron. The CSG commander is responsible for the tactical employment of the strike group during forward-deployed operations.

faqs.question: Is RADM equivalent to an Army Major General?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Navy Rear Admiral (O-8) is equivalent in paygrade and seniority to a Major General in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force.

sources.label: U.S. Fleet Forces Command — Carrier Strike Groups

name: Vice Admiral
insignia_alt: Three silver stars — U.S. Navy Vice Admiral flag insignia
meta_title: Vice Admiral (VADM / O-9) — U.S. Navy Three-Star Flag Officer | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Vice Admiral (VADM) is the U.S. Navy three-star flag officer rank at paygrade O-9 — commanders of Numbered Fleets and senior Pentagon and Joint Staff billets.
hero_tagline: The Navy's three-star flag officer — Numbered Fleet commanders and senior service chiefs.
overview:
Vice Admiral (VADM) is the U.S. Navy O-9 flag officer rank — a three-star admiral, equivalent in paygrade to a Lieutenant General in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. VADMs command Numbered Fleets (e.g., U.S. 3rd Fleet, U.S. 5th Fleet, U.S. 7th Fleet), serve as Deputy Chief of Naval Operations on the OPNAV staff, command Naval Forces Cyber Command, and hold senior positions at U.S. and combatant commands.

Unlike permanent O-1 through O-6 ranks, three-star (O-9) and four-star (O-10) positions are tied to specific billets. An officer holds the grade only while serving in a position designated for that grade by Congress.
history:
The rank of Vice Admiral was authorized for the U.S. Navy in 1862 alongside the original creation of the Rear Admiral grade. The first U.S. Navy Vice Admiral was David Glasgow Farragut, who was promoted from Rear Admiral to Vice Admiral in 1864.

In modern practice, VADMs occupy the most senior operational and staff positions in the Navy short of full Admiral. The number of three-star billets in each service is set annually by the Department of Defense and subject to statutory caps under 10 U.S.C.
responsibilities: Commander of a Numbered Fleet (e.g., U.S. 3rd, 5th, 6th, 7th, 10th Fleet)
Deputy Chief of Naval Operations (e.g., DCNO for Operations, Plans, Strategy)
Commander, Naval Air Forces (AIRPAC) or Commander, Naval Surface Forces (SURFPAC)
Senior leader at a Combatant Command (e.g., Deputy Commander, USINDOPACOM)
addressing: Verbally "Admiral Smith." In writing: "VADM Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by a flag-officer promotion board and Senate confirmation
Successful service at the O-8 grade
Position-tied promotion: must be assigned to an O-9 billet authorized by Congress
common_assignments: Commander, U.S. Third Fleet (San Diego, CA)
Commander, U.S. Seventh Fleet (Yokosuka, Japan)
Deputy Chief of Naval Operations on the OPNAV staff (Pentagon)
Commander, Naval Air Forces / Naval Surface Forces

pay_range.note: Statutory pay cap applies — flag-officer basic pay is capped at the rate prescribed by 5 U.S.C. § 5316 (Executive Schedule Level III) regardless of years of service.

related_base_note: U.S. Pacific Fleet Numbered Fleet commanders (VADMs) are headquartered in the Pacific theater, including Pearl Harbor.

faqs.question: How many Vice Admirals serve in the U.S. Navy?
faqs.answer: The number of active-duty Vice Admirals is set by Department of Defense allocations under statutory caps. The Navy typically has roughly 30–40 three-star officers serving in operational and staff billets at any given time.

faqs.question: Is VADM equivalent to an Army Lieutenant General?
faqs.answer: Yes. A Navy Vice Admiral (O-9) is equivalent in paygrade and seniority to a Lieutenant General in the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force.

name: Admiral
insignia_alt: Four silver stars — U.S. Navy Admiral flag insignia
meta_title: Admiral (ADM / O-10) — U.S. Navy Four-Star Flag Officer | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Admiral (ADM, O-10) — the Navy's highest active-duty flag rank, held by the CNO and combatant commanders. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's four-star flag officer — Chief of Naval Operations and Navy Combatant Commanders.
overview:
Admiral (ADM) is the highest active-duty rank in the U.S. Navy at paygrade O-10 — a four-star admiral, equivalent in paygrade to a General in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force. The Navy is authorized a small number of four-star billets at any given time, including the Chief of Naval Operations (CNO), the Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO), Combatant Commanders who are Navy officers (e.g., USINDOPACOM, USTRANSCOM), and Component Commanders (USFLTFORCOM, USPACFLT).

Like the three-star Vice Admiral grade, four-star Admiral is a position-tied rank — an officer holds the grade only while assigned to an O-10 billet authorized by Congress.
history:
Congress first authorized the rank of Admiral for the U.S. Navy in 1866, promoting David Glasgow Farragut to the grade in recognition of his Civil War service. The grade was used sparingly until World War II, when Congress authorized the senior wartime ranks to recognize fleet and theater commanders.

The grade above Admiral — Fleet Admiral (five stars) — was created during World War II for William D. Leahy, Ernest J. King, Chester W. Nimitz, and William F. Halsey, Jr. No officer has held five-star rank since Fleet Admiral Halsey's death in 1959, and the grade is currently dormant.
responsibilities: Chief of Naval Operations (CNO) — senior uniformed officer of the U.S. Navy and member of the Joint Chiefs of Staff
Vice Chief of Naval Operations (VCNO)
Combatant Commander (e.g., Commander, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command)
Navy Component Commander (Commander, U.S. Fleet Forces Command; Commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet)
addressing: Verbally "Admiral Smith." In writing: "ADM Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Nomination by the President and confirmation by the U.S. Senate
Position-tied promotion: must be assigned to an O-10 billet authorized by Congress
Successful service at the O-9 grade
common_assignments: Chief of Naval Operations (CNO), Pentagon
Commander, U.S. Indo-Pacific Command (USINDOPACOM), Camp H.M. Smith, HI
Commander, U.S. Fleet Forces Command (USFFC), Norfolk, VA
Commander, U.S. Pacific Fleet (USPACFLT), Pearl Harbor, HI

pay_range.note: Statutory pay cap applies — flag-officer basic pay is capped at Executive Schedule Level III (5 U.S.C. § 5316).

related_base_note: U.S. Pacific Fleet, headquartered at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, is commanded by a four-star Admiral.

faqs.question: How many four-star Admirals are there in the U.S. Navy?
faqs.answer: The U.S. Navy is typically authorized roughly 6–10 active-duty four-star Admirals at any given time, including the Chief of Naval Operations, the Vice Chief of Naval Operations, Combatant Commanders, and Component Commanders. The exact number depends on current Department of Defense allocations.

faqs.question: Is there a five-star rank in the U.S. Navy?
faqs.answer: Yes — Fleet Admiral (five stars) was created during World War II. The rank has been dormant since the death of Fleet Admiral William F. Halsey, Jr. in 1959, and no officer currently holds five-star rank.

name: Warrant Officer 1
insignia_alt: Navy-blue bar with two narrow gold breaks — Navy Warrant Officer 1 collar device
meta_title: Warrant Officer 1 (WO1 / W-1) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Warrant Officer 1 (WO1, W-1) — the Navy's entry-grade warrant rank, appointed by warrant of the Secretary of the Navy. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
hero_tagline: The Navy's entry-grade warrant officer — a single-track technical specialist appointed by warrant.
overview:
Warrant Officer 1 (WO1) is the entry-level warrant officer rank in the U.S. Navy at paygrade W-1. Warrant officers are highly skilled, single-track technical specialists drawn from the senior enlisted ranks. Unlike commissioned officers — who are commissioned by the President — Warrant Officer 1s are appointed by warrant of the Secretary of the Navy. WO1 is rarely used in the modern Navy; the service typically appoints qualified senior enlisted Sailors directly to Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2). The grade remains on the books and is included in this directory for completeness.

Warrant officers fill specialized billets — engineering, intelligence, cyber, special operations, ordnance — where deep technical expertise must be retained beyond the typical enlisted career arc.
history:
Congress authorized the warrant officer program in the modern U.S. military in 1916 and rebuilt it after World War II. The U.S. Navy's contemporary warrant officer program is governed by 10 U.S.C. and Navy regulations, which permit appointment of qualified Chief Petty Officers, Senior Chief Petty Officers, and Master Chief Petty Officers as warrant officers in technical specialties.

Although the W-1 grade is statutorily authorized, the U.S. Navy has not appointed officers to W-1 in routine practice for many years; new warrant officers are typically appointed directly to CWO2.
responsibilities: Provide technical leadership in a specialized field (engineering, ordnance, cryptology, etc.)
Mentor enlisted Sailors in their technical community
Advise commanding officers on technical matters within their specialty
addressing: Verbally "Mister/Miss Smith" or "Warrant Officer Smith." In writing: "WO1 Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Senior enlisted rating (typically E-7 and above) with strong technical record
Selection by the warrant officer accession board
Appointment by warrant of the Secretary of the Navy
common_assignments: Technical specialist billets within a community
Shipboard or shore-based subject-matter expert

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table — W-1 grade.

related_base_note: Navy warrant officers serve in technical billets across the fleet, including ships homeported at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: Does the Navy actively appoint Warrant Officer 1s?
faqs.answer: Not in routine practice. The U.S. Navy typically appoints qualified senior enlisted Sailors directly to Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2). The W-1 grade remains statutorily authorized but is rarely used in the modern Navy.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a warrant officer and a commissioned officer?
faqs.answer: Commissioned officers are commissioned by the President and serve in a wide range of operational and command billets. Warrant officers are appointed by the Secretary of the Navy as single-track technical specialists, drawn from the senior enlisted ranks.

name: Chief Warrant Officer 2
insignia_alt: Gold bar with two narrow blue breaks — Navy Chief Warrant Officer 2 collar device
meta_title: Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2 / W-2) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2, W-2) — the Navy's entry commissioned warrant rank, drawn from senior enlisted. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
h1: Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2) — U.S. Navy W-2
hero_tagline: The Navy's entry-level commissioned warrant officer — appointed from the senior enlisted ranks.
overview:
Chief Warrant Officer 2 (CWO2) is the entry-level commissioned warrant officer rank in the U.S. Navy at paygrade W-2. Unlike WO1, who is appointed by warrant of the Secretary of the Navy, CWO2s are commissioned by the President. In practice, the Navy appoints qualified Chief Petty Officers, Senior Chief Petty Officers, and Master Chief Petty Officers directly to CWO2, skipping the W-1 grade.

Chief Warrant Officers serve as single-track technical specialists in fields such as Surface Operations, Aviation Maintenance, Information Warfare, Cryptology, Special Operations, Engineering, Ordnance, and Diving. CWO2s typically lead small technical teams, advise commanding officers on technical matters, and mentor enlisted Sailors in their community.
history:
The Chief Warrant Officer 2 grade was created in its modern form by the Warrant Officer Management Act of 1991, which restructured the warrant officer ranks across the Department of Defense. The Navy's CWO accession path draws qualified senior enlisted Sailors with at least 12 years of service and exceptional technical performance into the warrant officer community.

The Navy's Limited Duty Officer (LDO) program is a related but separate accession path that commissions senior enlisted Sailors as restricted commissioned officers (O-1E through O-6) in technical specialties.
responsibilities: Lead a small technical team in a specialty field
Advise the chain of command on technical matters within their community
Mentor and train enlisted Sailors in advanced technical skills
Stand technical-specialty watches afloat or ashore as required
addressing: Verbally "Mister/Miss Smith" or "Chief Warrant Officer Smith." In writing: "CWO2 Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Typically 12+ years of enlisted service at the E-6 (PO1), E-7 (CPO), E-8 (SCPO), or E-9 (MCPO) grade
Selection by the Navy CWO accession board
Commission by the President of the United States
common_assignments: Surface Ordnance Technician CWO aboard a destroyer or amphibious ship
Aviation Maintenance CWO at a fleet squadron or air station
Cryptologic Warfare Technician CWO at a Navy Information Operations Command
Diving Officer at an EOD or salvage unit

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table — W-2 grade.

related_base_note: Many Pacific Fleet CWOs serve aboard surface combatants homeported at Naval Base San Diego.

faqs.question: How does a Sailor become a CWO2?
faqs.answer: A Navy Sailor must typically have at least 12 years of enlisted service at the E-6 grade or above and be selected by the annual CWO accession board. CWO2 is the typical entry grade for new warrant officers in the U.S. Navy.

faqs.question: Is a CWO2 a commissioned officer?
faqs.answer: Yes. CWO2 and above are commissioned warrant officers, commissioned by the President. WO1 is the only Navy warrant grade appointed by warrant of the Secretary of the Navy and is rarely used.

name: Chief Warrant Officer 3
insignia_alt: Gold bar with three narrow blue breaks — Navy Chief Warrant Officer 3 collar device
meta_title: Chief Warrant Officer 3 (CWO3 / W-3) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Chief Warrant Officer 3 (CWO3, W-3) — the Navy's mid-grade commissioned warrant rank for senior technical experts. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
h1: Chief Warrant Officer 3 (CWO3) — U.S. Navy W-3
hero_tagline: The Navy's mid-grade commissioned warrant officer — senior technical specialists.
overview:
Chief Warrant Officer 3 (CWO3) is the U.S. Navy commissioned warrant officer rank at paygrade W-3. Promotion from CWO2 to CWO3 is by selection board, typically after 5–6 years of warrant-officer service. CWO3s assume increasingly senior technical leadership roles and may supervise other warrant officers and senior enlisted Sailors.

CWO3s frequently serve as the senior technical specialist in their community at a major command, lead instructor at a Navy "C"-school, or technical advisor at a Type Commander or Numbered Fleet staff.
history:
The CWO3 grade was reorganized by the Warrant Officer Management Act of 1991 along with the rest of the warrant officer pay grades. Promotion progressions from CWO2 to CWO3, CWO4, and CWO5 mirror commissioned officer promotion timelines.

Modern Navy warrant officer specialties include Surface Operations, Aviation Maintenance, Aviation Operations, Engineering, Information Warfare, Cryptologic Warfare, Intelligence, Civil Engineering, EOD, Diver, Special Warfare, Operations Technician, and Bandmaster — among others.
responsibilities: Senior technical specialist in a community at a major command
Lead instructor at a Navy "C"-school or Center of Excellence
Technical advisor at a Type Commander or Numbered Fleet staff
Mentor junior CWOs and senior enlisted leaders
addressing: Verbally "Mister/Miss Smith" or "Chief Warrant Officer Smith." In writing: "CWO3 Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by the CWO3 promotion board
Approximately 5–6 years of service as a CWO2
common_assignments: Senior Cryptologic Warfare CWO at a Navy Information Operations Command
Aviation Maintenance CWO3 at a Fleet Replacement Squadron
Surface Operations CWO3 aboard a flagship
Senior instructor at the Surface Warfare Officers School

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table — W-3 grade.

related_base_note: Senior Atlantic Fleet warrant officers serve at flagships and major commands at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: How long does it take to promote from CWO2 to CWO3?
faqs.answer: A CWO2 typically becomes eligible for promotion to CWO3 after approximately 5–6 years of warrant-officer service. Promotion is by Navy selection board.

name: Chief Warrant Officer 4
insignia_alt: Gold bar with four narrow blue breaks — Navy Chief Warrant Officer 4 collar device
meta_title: Chief Warrant Officer 4 (CWO4 / W-4) — U.S. Navy Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Chief Warrant Officer 4 (CWO4, W-4) — the Navy's senior commissioned warrant rank and top technical authority. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
h1: Chief Warrant Officer 4 (CWO4) — U.S. Navy W-4
hero_tagline: The Navy's senior commissioned warrant officer — top technical authority in their specialty.
overview:
Chief Warrant Officer 4 (CWO4) is the U.S. Navy commissioned warrant officer rank at paygrade W-4. Promotion to CWO4 is by selection board after approximately 5–6 years as a CWO3. CWO4s are typically the senior technical specialist in their community at a major command — Type Commander staff, Numbered Fleet staff, or major shore activity.

CWO4s often hold billets such as Force Cryptologic Warfare Technician, Force Maintenance Officer, or senior technical advisor to a Carrier Strike Group commander.
history:
The CWO4 grade was set by the Warrant Officer Management Act of 1991 and is the senior commissioned warrant officer grade for most warrant officer communities. The CWO5 grade was added later as a capstone grade for the most experienced warrant officers.

Promotion to CWO4 historically runs at high opportunity rates for officers in the primary zone, reflecting the Navy's investment in retaining its most experienced technical specialists.
responsibilities: Senior technical specialist in their community at a major command
Force-level technical advisor at Type Commander or Numbered Fleet staff
Lead instructor at a Navy Center of Excellence
Mentor junior warrant officers and senior enlisted leaders
addressing: Verbally "Mister/Miss Smith" or "Chief Warrant Officer Smith." In writing: "CWO4 Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by the CWO4 promotion board
Approximately 5–6 years of service as a CWO3
common_assignments: Force Cryptologic Warfare Technician at a Type Commander staff
Force Maintenance Officer at NAVAIR or a Type Commander
Senior technical advisor at a Numbered Fleet or Combatant Command
Master instructor at a Surface, Submarine, or Aviation school

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table — W-4 grade.

related_base_note: Senior Pacific Fleet CWOs serve at Type Commander staffs based in San Diego.

faqs.question: Is CWO4 the highest warrant officer rank?
faqs.answer: No. The Navy authorizes a fifth commissioned warrant officer grade — Chief Warrant Officer 5 (CWO5) — as the capstone of the warrant-officer career path. CWO4 is the second-most-senior warrant grade.

name: Chief Warrant Officer 5
insignia_alt: Silver bar with vertical blue stripe — Navy Chief Warrant Officer 5 collar device
meta_title: Chief Warrant Officer 5 (CWO5 / W-5) — U.S. Navy Capstone Warrant Rank | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Chief Warrant Officer 5 (CWO5) is the most senior U.S. Navy commissioned warrant officer rank at paygrade W-5 — the capstone of the warrant officer career path.
h1: Chief Warrant Officer 5 (CWO5) — U.S. Navy W-5
hero_tagline: The Navy's most senior warrant officer — the capstone of the technical-specialist career path.
overview:
Chief Warrant Officer 5 (CWO5) is the most senior commissioned warrant officer rank in the U.S. Navy at paygrade W-5. Promotion to CWO5 is highly competitive, with only a small number of warrant officers selected each year. CWO5s serve in the most senior technical-advisor billets in their community — typically at Numbered Fleet, Type Commander, or OPNAV staffs.

The Navy uses CWO5 as a capstone grade reserved for the very best of its warrant-officer corps. CWO5s are often the senior technical authority in their entire community.
history:
Congress authorized the CWO5 grade in 1991 as a capstone warrant officer rank, providing a final promotion opportunity for the most exceptional warrant officers. The Navy began appointing officers to CWO5 in 2002.

Each warrant officer community elects a small number of CWO5 billets, typically at the Force level (e.g., Force Cryptologic Warrant Officer, Force Aviation Maintenance Officer).
responsibilities: Senior technical authority in their community Navy-wide
Force-level technical advisor at Type Commander, Numbered Fleet, or OPNAV
Senior representative for their warrant-officer community on personnel matters
Mentor and develop the next generation of senior warrant officers
addressing: Verbally "Mister/Miss Smith" or "Chief Warrant Officer Smith." In writing: "CWO5 Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: Selection by the CWO5 promotion board
Approximately 5–6 years of service as a CWO4
Exceptional sustained technical and leadership performance
common_assignments: Force Warrant Officer at a Type Commander (e.g., Surface Forces, Air Forces)
Senior technical advisor on the OPNAV staff
Senior community manager at MyNavyHR (BUPERS)

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table — W-5 grade.

related_base_note: Force Warrant Officers serve at Atlantic Fleet Type Commander headquarters in Norfolk.

faqs.question: How many CWO5s are in the U.S. Navy?
faqs.answer: The number is small — typically only a handful of CWO5s are selected each year, and the total active-duty population at any time is in the low hundreds across all warrant officer communities.

name: Seaman Recruit
insignia_alt: No rate insignia — U.S. Navy Seaman Recruit (E-1) wears no rating mark
meta_title: Seaman Recruit (SR / E-1) — U.S. Navy Enlisted Paygrade | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Seaman Recruit (SR) is the entry-level U.S. Navy enlisted paygrade at E-1 — the rank held by recruits during boot camp at Recruit Training Command, Great Lakes.
hero_tagline: The Navy's entry-level enlisted paygrade — boot camp recruits and newly accessed Sailors.
overview:
Seaman Recruit (SR) is the U.S. Navy's entry-level enlisted paygrade at E-1. Most new enlisted Sailors enter the Navy as Seaman Recruits and remain in the grade through Recruit Training Command (RTC), Great Lakes, Illinois — the Navy's only enlisted boot camp. Seaman Recruits wear no rate insignia on the dress uniform; the absence of a rating mark visually signals their entry-level status.

Most Seaman Recruits promote automatically to Seaman Apprentice (E-2) after approximately nine months of satisfactory service, often coinciding with completion of "A"-school technical training and report to their first fleet command.
history:
The "Seaman Recruit" title in its modern form dates to mid-20th-century U.S. Navy reorganization of enlisted ratings and paygrades. The Navy has used the broader "seaman" designation for un-rated enlisted Sailors for centuries — drawing on age-of-sail terminology that distinguished an "ordinary seaman" or "able seaman" from a rated specialist.

The Navy's only enlisted accession point — Recruit Training Command, Great Lakes — has trained more than 4 million Sailors since opening in 1911 and is the singular gateway through which every active and reserve enlisted Sailor enters the U.S. Navy.
responsibilities: Complete Recruit Training (boot camp) at RTC Great Lakes
Master basic Sailor skills: drill, watchstanding, military bearing, damage control
Begin "A"-school or report to first fleet command after graduation
addressing: Verbally "Seaman Recruit Smith" or "Seaman Smith." In writing: "SR Jane Smith, USN."
prerequisites: U.S. citizenship or permanent residency
High school diploma or GED equivalent
Successful completion of MEPS processing and ASVAB testing
common_assignments: Recruit Training Command (RTC), Great Lakes, IL — boot camp
Navy "A"-school student in their selected rating
Newly reported Sailor at first sea or shore command

related_base_note: Every U.S. Navy enlisted Sailor begins their career as a Seaman Recruit at Recruit Training Command, Naval Station Great Lakes.

faqs.question: How long does a Sailor remain a Seaman Recruit?
faqs.answer: Most Seaman Recruits promote to Seaman Apprentice (E-2) after approximately nine months of satisfactory service, which typically coincides with completion of boot camp and "A"-school training.

faqs.question: Where does a Seaman Recruit go to boot camp?
faqs.answer: Every U.S. Navy enlisted Sailor — active and reserve — attends boot camp at Recruit Training Command (RTC), Great Lakes, Illinois. RTC Great Lakes is the Navy's only enlisted accession point.

name: Seaman Apprentice
insignia_alt: Two diagonal stripes — U.S. Navy Seaman Apprentice (E-2) rate insignia
meta_title: Seaman Apprentice (SA / E-2) — U.S. Navy Enlisted Paygrade | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Seaman Apprentice (SA, E-2) — the Navy's second enlisted paygrade, with community variants SA, FA, AA, CA, and HA. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
hero_tagline: The Navy's second-tier enlisted paygrade — apprentice Sailors of all general apprenticeships.
overview:
Seaman Apprentice (SA) is the U.S. Navy E-2 enlisted paygrade. The "Seaman Apprentice" title is the most common variant; the Navy uses several community-specific apprentice titles at E-2 depending on the Sailor's general apprenticeship: Seaman Apprentice (SA, deck and admin), Fireman Apprentice (FA, engineering), Airman Apprentice (AN to AA — aviation), Constructionman Apprentice (CA, Seabees), and Hospitalman Apprentice (HA, hospital corps). All five share paygrade E-2 and the same two-stripe insignia.

Most Seaman Apprentices promote to Seaman (E-3) after approximately nine months of additional satisfactory service.
history:
The Navy formalized its general-apprenticeship community structure in the mid-20th century, codifying the distinct apprentice tracks that funnel new Sailors toward the rated specialty (rating) they will eventually hold. Each apprenticeship — Seaman, Fireman, Airman, Constructionman, Hospitalman — corresponds to a broad fleet community and culminates in a specific E-4 rating ("striker") within that community.

The differentiated titles are a uniquely Navy construct that traces back to age-of-sail rating practices, where the Sailor's job title changed depending on whether they worked on deck, below decks, or in a specialty.
responsibilities: Continue developing rating-specific technical skills
Stand entry-level shipboard or shore watches
Work toward "striker" qualification in the chosen rating
addressing: Verbally "Seaman Apprentice Smith" or "Seaman Smith." In writing: "SA Jane Smith, USN" — or the appropriate community variant (FA, AA, CA, HA).
prerequisites: Approximately 9 months of satisfactory service as a Seaman Recruit
Time-in-rate met for advancement to E-2
common_assignments: Junior Sailor aboard surface combatant, submarine, or auxiliary
Apprentice in an aviation squadron or Seabee battalion
Hospital Corpsman apprentice at a Navy medical facility

related_base_note: Many newly promoted Seaman Apprentices begin "A"-school in the Great Lakes training complex.

Engineering apprentices headed toward ratings such as MM, EN, GSM, or HT.
Aviation apprentices headed toward ratings such as AT, AE, AM, or AO.
Naval Construction Force apprentices headed toward ratings such as BU, CE, EO, or SW.
Hospital Corpsman apprentices headed toward the HM rating.

faqs.question: Why do some E-2 Sailors have different titles?
faqs.answer: The Navy uses five community-variant titles at the E-2 paygrade — Seaman Apprentice (SA), Fireman Apprentice (FA), Airman Apprentice (AA), Constructionman Apprentice (CA), and Hospitalman Apprentice (HA) — depending on the Sailor's general apprenticeship community. All five share paygrade E-2 and the same two-stripe insignia.

faqs.question: How long does a Sailor remain a Seaman Apprentice?
faqs.answer: A Seaman Apprentice typically promotes to Seaman (E-3) after approximately nine months of additional satisfactory service.

name: Seaman
insignia_alt: Three diagonal stripes — U.S. Navy Seaman (E-3) rate insignia
meta_title: Seaman (SN / E-3) — U.S. Navy Enlisted Paygrade | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Seaman (SN, E-3) — the Navy's highest un-rated enlisted paygrade, where strikers prepare to earn a rating. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
hero_tagline: The Navy's third-tier enlisted paygrade — strikers preparing to earn a rating.
overview:
Seaman (SN) is the U.S. Navy E-3 enlisted paygrade — the highest un-rated grade. Like E-2, E-3 uses five community-variant titles depending on the Sailor's general apprenticeship: Seaman (SN), Fireman (FN), Airman (AN), Constructionman (CN), and Hospitalman (HN). All five share paygrade E-3 and the same three-stripe insignia.

Most Seamen promote to Petty Officer Third Class (E-4) only by passing a competitive Navy-wide advancement exam in their selected rating. E-3 to E-4 is the first non-automatic enlisted promotion in the U.S. Navy career path.
history:
The "Seaman" rating designation in its modern form was standardized in the mid-20th century. Historically the U.S. Navy used grades such as Ordinary Seaman, Able Seaman, and Seaman First Class — descended directly from age-of-sail British Royal Navy practice. The 1948 enlisted rating reform consolidated the apprentice grades into the modern SR, SA, SN structure familiar today.

E-3 is the typical paygrade at which a Sailor "strikes" for a rating — that is, formally trains for and applies to enter a specific specialty community such as Boatswain's Mate (BM), Operations Specialist (OS), or Hospital Corpsman (HM).
responsibilities: Strike for a Navy rating by completing on-the-job training and qualifications
Stand watch in an assigned division aboard ship or ashore
Begin preparing for the Navy-wide E-4 advancement exam
addressing: Verbally "Seaman Smith." In writing: "SN Jane Smith, USN" — or the appropriate community variant (FN, AN, CN, HN).
prerequisites: Approximately 9 months of satisfactory service as a Seaman Apprentice
Time-in-rate met for advancement to E-3
common_assignments: Striker in an assigned division aboard a fleet unit
Apprentice technician in a fleet aviation squadron
Hospital Corpsman apprentice at a Navy medical facility or with a Marine Corps unit

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: Many Atlantic Fleet Seamen serve their first sea tour aboard ships homeported at Naval Station Norfolk.

community_variants.description: Default Seaman community — strikers for ratings such as BM, OS, QM, YN, or PS.
Engineering strikers headed toward ratings such as MM, EN, GSM, or HT.
Aviation strikers headed toward ratings such as AT, AE, AM, or AO.
Naval Construction Force strikers headed toward ratings such as BU, CE, EO, or SW.
Hospital Corpsman strikers headed toward the HM rating.

faqs.question: How does a Seaman become a Petty Officer?
faqs.answer: Promotion from E-3 to Petty Officer Third Class (E-4) is the first competitive advancement in the U.S. Navy enlisted career path. A Seaman must pass a Navy-wide advancement exam in their selected rating, meet time-in-rate requirements, and earn satisfactory evaluations to be advanced.

faqs.question: What is the difference between SN, FN, AN, CN, and HN?
faqs.answer: All five are E-3 paygrade titles. SN (Seaman) is the default deck/admin community, FN (Fireman) is engineering, AN (Airman) is aviation, CN (Constructionman) is the Seabees, and HN (Hospitalman) is the Hospital Corps. Each leads to a distinct family of E-4 ratings.

name: Petty Officer Third Class
insignia_alt: Eagle over one chevron with rating mark — U.S. Navy Petty Officer Third Class crow
meta_title: Petty Officer Third Class (PO3 / E-4) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Petty Officer Third Class (PO3, E-4) — the Navy's first petty officer grade and first rated paygrade. Insignia, pay, history, and how to address one.
h1: Petty Officer Third Class (PO3) — U.S. Navy E-4
hero_tagline: The Navy's entry-level non-commissioned officer — the first rated grade.
overview:
Petty Officer Third Class (PO3) is the U.S. Navy E-4 enlisted paygrade — the Navy's first non-commissioned officer (NCO) grade. The transition from un-rated Seaman to rated Petty Officer is a major career milestone: the Sailor now holds a specific Navy rating (e.g., Boatswain's Mate, Operations Specialist, Hospital Corpsman), wears the rating mark on their crow, and is referred to formally by their rating combined with their paygrade — for example, "Operations Specialist Third Class (OS3)."

Promotion from E-3 to E-4 is the first competitive enlisted advancement in the U.S. Navy. It requires passing a Navy-wide advancement-in-rate examination, satisfactory evaluations, and meeting time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums.
history:
The Navy has used the term "Petty Officer" since the founding of the service, drawing on British Royal Navy practice. "Petty" comes from the French "petit" (small), and historically referred to ship's specialists who held minor authority but were not commissioned officers. The "crow" insignia — an eagle over chevrons — was adopted in 1885 and remains one of the most recognizable enlisted devices in any U.S. military uniform.

The modern rating structure dates to the 1948 enlisted reorganization, which consolidated more than 100 specialty ratings into the cleaner family of communities used today.
responsibilities: Lead a small work center or watch team
Train and supervise junior Sailors (E-1 through E-3)
Perform rating-specific technical work to qualified standards
Pursue Enlisted Surface, Submarine, or Aviation Warfare qualification
addressing: Verbally "Petty Officer Smith." In writing: rating + grade + name (e.g., "OS3 Jane Smith, USN").
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-4 advancement exam in selected rating
Time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums per OPNAVINST
Satisfactory evaluations
common_assignments: Work-center supervisor in an assigned division
Watch-team leader in CIC, engineering, deck, or aviation maintenance
Rated technician aboard ship, in an aviation squadron, or at a shore command

faqs.question: What is a "rating" in the U.S. Navy?
faqs.answer: A rating is the Navy's term for an enlisted specialty community — for example, Boatswain's Mate (BM), Operations Specialist (OS), Hospital Corpsman (HM), or Aviation Electronics Technician (AT). A Sailor formally holds a rating starting at E-4.

faqs.question: Is a Petty Officer Third Class an NCO?
faqs.answer: Yes. The U.S. Navy considers all Petty Officers — E-4 (PO3), E-5 (PO2), and E-6 (PO1) — to be non-commissioned officers (NCOs).

name: Petty Officer Second Class
insignia_alt: Eagle over two chevrons with rating mark — U.S. Navy Petty Officer Second Class crow
meta_title: Petty Officer Second Class (PO2 / E-5) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Petty Officer Second Class (PO2, E-5) — the Navy's mid-grade petty officer, leading work centers and senior watches. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
h1: Petty Officer Second Class (PO2) — U.S. Navy E-5
hero_tagline: The Navy's mid-grade non-commissioned officer — work-center supervisors and senior watchstanders.
overview:
Petty Officer Second Class (PO2) is the U.S. Navy E-5 enlisted paygrade. Promotion from PO3 to PO2 is competitive and requires passing the Navy-wide E-5 advancement exam, satisfactory evaluations, and time-in-rate. PO2s typically supervise multi-person work centers, lead complex shipboard or aviation maintenance evolutions, and are routinely qualified as senior watchstanders.

PO2s are addressed by their rating and paygrade — for example, "Operations Specialist Second Class (OS2)." They wear the rating mark on a crow consisting of an eagle over two chevrons.
history:
The "Second Class" Petty Officer designation dates to the U.S. Navy's mid-19th-century reorganization of enlisted grades. The two-chevron PO2 crow has been worn in roughly its current form since 1885.

The PO2 grade is widely considered the Navy's first true "supervisory NCO" grade — PO2s are the Sailors most commonly entrusted with running a discrete work center on their own.
responsibilities: Supervise a multi-Sailor work center
Lead routine and complex shipboard or aviation maintenance evolutions
Stand qualified senior watch as Engineering Officer of the Watch (EOOW) candidate, CIC Watch Officer, or aviation maintenance shift supervisor
Mentor and develop junior Petty Officers and Seamen
addressing: Verbally "Petty Officer Smith." In writing: rating + grade + name (e.g., "OS2 Jane Smith, USN").
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-5 advancement exam in selected rating
Time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums per OPNAVINST
Satisfactory evaluations and warfare-qualification progress
common_assignments: Work-center supervisor in an assigned shipboard division
Senior watchstander in CIC, engineering, or aviation maintenance
"A"-school or "C"-school instructor at a Navy training command

related_base_note: PO2s serve as work-center supervisors aboard ships homeported at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: How is a PO2 addressed?
faqs.answer: A Petty Officer Second Class is addressed verbally as "Petty Officer Smith." In writing, the Sailor's rating and paygrade are combined into a title like "OS2" (Operations Specialist Second Class) or "HM2" (Hospital Corpsman Second Class).

name: Petty Officer First Class
insignia_alt: Eagle over three chevrons with rating mark — U.S. Navy Petty Officer First Class crow
meta_title: Petty Officer First Class (PO1 / E-6) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Petty Officer First Class (PO1, E-6) — the Navy's senior petty officer grade below Chief, the LPO of large divisions. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
h1: Petty Officer First Class (PO1) — U.S. Navy E-6
hero_tagline: The Navy's senior non-commissioned officer — leading petty officers of major divisions.
overview:
Petty Officer First Class (PO1) is the U.S. Navy E-6 enlisted paygrade. PO1s are the most senior non-commissioned officers below the Chief Petty Officer mess and are typically the Leading Petty Officer (LPO) of a major shipboard or shore division. The PO1 grade is also the lowest from which a Sailor can be selected for the Chief Warrant Officer or Limited Duty Officer (LDO) commissioning programs.

PO1s wear the rating mark on a crow consisting of an eagle over three chevrons. Promotion to E-6 is competitive and requires the Navy-wide advancement exam, satisfactory evaluations, and time-in-rate.
history:
The "First Class" designation has been used in the U.S. Navy enlisted structure since the late 19th century. PO1 is the senior non-commissioned grade in the modern Navy — the next promotion, to Chief Petty Officer (E-7), brings a Sailor across the storied "Chief's mess" threshold and into the Navy's senior enlisted leadership.

PO1 is the typical paygrade from which Sailors apply for the Chief Warrant Officer accession program or the Limited Duty Officer commissioning program.

Mentor and develop the entire division's junior Petty Officers and Seamen
Run rating-specific technical evolutions to qualified standards
Eligible for Chief Warrant Officer or Limited Duty Officer accession boards
addressing: Verbally "Petty Officer Smith." In writing: rating + grade + name (e.g., "OS1 Jane Smith, USN").
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-6 advancement exam in selected rating
Time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums
Satisfactory evaluations and warfare-qualification status

Senior watchstander on the Navy's most demanding watches
Senior instructor at an "A"- or "C"-school
Detailer at MyNavyHR (BUPERS), Millington, TN

faqs.question: What is a Leading Petty Officer (LPO)?
faqs.answer: The Leading Petty Officer (LPO) is the senior enlisted Sailor in a shipboard or shore division below the rank of Chief Petty Officer. The LPO billet is most often filled by a PO1.

name: Chief Petty Officer
insignia_alt: Gold rocker over three gold chevrons with eagle and rating mark — U.S. Navy Chief Petty Officer fouled-anchor device
meta_title: Chief Petty Officer (CPO / E-7) — U.S. Navy Senior Enlisted | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Chief Petty Officer (CPO, E-7) — entry into the Navy's storied Chief's mess, marked by gold fouled anchors and khakis. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
h1: Chief Petty Officer (CPO) — U.S. Navy E-7
hero_tagline: The Navy's senior enlisted leader — the storied "Chief's mess."
overview:
Chief Petty Officer (CPO) is the U.S. Navy E-7 enlisted paygrade — the entry grade into the Navy's storied "Chief's mess," the senior enlisted leadership corps. The transition to Chief is one of the most distinctive milestones in any U.S. military service: selectees undergo a six-week "Chief's Initiation Season" culminating in a "pinning" ceremony where the Sailor receives gold fouled anchors and dons the iconic Khaki uniform reserved for Chiefs and officers.

CPOs are the Navy's principal enlisted leaders — running shipboard departments, mentoring junior officers, and serving as the institutional memory of their rating. The CPO uniform difference (Khakis instead of dungarees/working uniform), the distinct insignia (fouled anchors instead of the petty-officer crow), and the dedicated "Chief's mess" aboard ship visually mark the rank as a class apart.
history:
The Chief Petty Officer rank was established by Congress on April 1, 1893, codifying a leadership grade that had existed informally aboard U.S. Navy ships since the founding of the service. The 1893 establishment date is celebrated annually as the CPO birthday.

The "fouled anchor" insignia worn by Chiefs — a vertical anchor with a chain twisted around it — is one of the oldest enlisted devices in any U.S. military service. The "USN" letters on the anchor were added in 1894. The Khaki uniform for Chiefs was adopted in 1941, deliberately distinguishing the CPO mess from the junior enlisted force.
responsibilities: Senior enlisted leader of a shipboard division or department
Mentor and develop junior Petty Officers and Seamen
Advise Division Officers and the Department Head on enlisted matters
Pursue qualification as Senior Enlisted Leader (SEL) of a unit
addressing: Verbally "Chief Smith." In writing: rating + grade + name (e.g., "OSC Jane Smith, USN" — note the "C" suffix for Chief).
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-7 advancement exam in selected rating
Selection by the Chief Petty Officer selection board
Successful completion of CPO Initiation (Khaki) Season
Time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums
common_assignments: Division Chief or Department LCPO aboard ship
Leading Chief Petty Officer at a fleet aviation squadron
Senior instructor at a Navy "A"- or "C"-school
Senior detailer at MyNavyHR (BUPERS)

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: CPO mess traditions are alive and well aboard the dozens of warships homeported at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: What makes the Chief Petty Officer rank unique?
faqs.answer: CPOs wear a distinct Khaki uniform (rather than the junior enlisted uniform), wear gold fouled anchors instead of the petty-officer crow, and belong to the "Chief's mess" — a culturally distinct senior enlisted leadership corps unique to the U.S. Navy and Coast Guard.

faqs.question: When is CPO birthday?
faqs.answer: The Chief Petty Officer rank was established by Congress on April 1, 1893. April 1 is celebrated annually as CPO Birthday across the fleet.

name: Senior Chief Petty Officer
insignia_alt: Chief Petty Officer device with one silver star above — U.S. Navy Senior Chief Petty Officer rate insignia
meta_title: Senior Chief Petty Officer (SCPO / E-8) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Senior Chief Petty Officer (SCPO) is the U.S. Navy E-8 senior enlisted paygrade — the second tier of the Chief's mess and a key adviser to commanding officers.
h1: Senior Chief Petty Officer (SCPO) — U.S. Navy E-8
hero_tagline: The Navy's second-tier Chief — senior enlisted leaders advising commanding officers.
overview:
Senior Chief Petty Officer (SCPO) is the U.S. Navy E-8 enlisted paygrade — the second tier of the Chief's mess. SCPOs typically serve as the Departmental Leading Chief Petty Officer (DLCPO) of a major shipboard department, the Command Senior Chief at a smaller unit, or the senior detailer for an entire rating community.

SCPOs wear the same fouled-anchor device as a CPO with one silver star above the anchors. Promotion from CPO to SCPO is by competitive selection board.
history:
Congress created the E-8 and E-9 paygrades in 1958, dividing the prior single Chief Petty Officer grade into three: Chief (E-7), Senior Chief (E-8), and Master Chief (E-9). The E-8/E-9 creation gave the Navy a clearer career progression and a more competitive senior enlisted promotion structure.

SCPOs and MCPOs are collectively referred to as the "senior enlisted" corps and provide the most experienced enlisted advice to commanding officers across the fleet.
responsibilities: Departmental Leading Chief Petty Officer (DLCPO) aboard ship
Command Senior Chief at a smaller shore or expeditionary command
Rating senior detailer at MyNavyHR (BUPERS)
Senior instructor or course manager at a Navy "C"-school
addressing: Verbally "Senior Chief Smith." In writing: rating + grade + name (e.g., "OSCS Jane Smith, USN" — note the "CS" suffix for Senior Chief).
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-8 advancement exam
Selection by the Senior Chief Petty Officer selection board
Time-in-rate and time-in-service minimums
common_assignments: DLCPO of a shipboard combat-systems, weapons, or engineering department
Command Senior Chief at a smaller unit
Rating Senior Detailer at BUPERS

pay_range.note: 2026 DFAS basic pay table.

related_base_note: Senior Chief detailers serve at MyNavyHR (BUPERS), Naval Support Activity Mid-South.

faqs.question: How is a Senior Chief addressed?
faqs.answer: A Senior Chief Petty Officer is addressed verbally as "Senior Chief Smith." In writing, the Sailor's rating, grade, and name are combined into a title like "OSCS" (Operations Specialist Senior Chief).

name: Master Chief Petty Officer
insignia_alt: Chief Petty Officer device with two silver stars above — U.S. Navy Master Chief Petty Officer rate insignia
meta_title: Master Chief Petty Officer (MCPO / E-9) — U.S. Navy | NavyWeek.org
meta_description: Master Chief Petty Officer (MCPO, E-9) — the Navy's most senior enlisted paygrade, with CMC, FLTCM, and MCPON billets. Insignia, pay, history, and addressing.
h1: Master Chief Petty Officer (MCPO) — U.S. Navy E-9
hero_tagline: The Navy's most senior enlisted leader — Command, Force, Fleet, and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy.
overview:
Master Chief Petty Officer (MCPO) is the U.S. Navy's most senior enlisted paygrade at E-9. MCPOs serve in the most senior enlisted billets in the Navy — Command Master Chief (CMC) at the unit level, Force Master Chief (FORCM) at Type Commander and Numbered Fleet level, Fleet Master Chief (FLTCM) at numbered fleet and component-command level, and Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) — the senior enlisted advisor to the Chief of Naval Operations.

MCPOs wear the fouled-anchor device with two silver stars above the anchors. Special-billet MCPOs (CMC, FORCM, FLTCM, MCPON) wear distinctive devices that incorporate gold stars and other symbols indicating their billet.
history:
Congress created the E-9 grade in 1958. The position of Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) was established in 1967 as the Navy's senior enlisted advisor to the Chief of Naval Operations and to the Secretary of the Navy.

The Force, Fleet, and Command Master Chief programs were formalized in subsequent decades to ensure a dedicated senior enlisted advisor to the commanding officer at every echelon — from a single ship up to the four-star fleet commander.
responsibilities: Command Master Chief (CMC) — senior enlisted advisor to a commanding officer at the unit level
Force Master Chief (FORCM) — senior enlisted advisor at a Type Commander or Numbered Fleet
Fleet Master Chief (FLTCM) — senior enlisted advisor at a numbered fleet or component command
Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) — senior enlisted advisor to the Chief of Naval Operations
addressing: Verbally "Master Chief Smith." MCPON is addressed as "MCPON" or "Master Chief." In writing: rating + grade (e.g., "OSCM Jane Smith, USN") for non-special-billet MCPOs.
prerequisites: Pass the Navy-wide E-9 advancement exam
Selection by the Master Chief Petty Officer selection board
Selection by separate panels for CMC, FORCM, FLTCM, and MCPON billets
common_assignments: Command Master Chief (CMC) at a ship, squadron, or shore command
Force Master Chief (FORCM) at a Type Commander headquarters
Fleet Master Chief (FLTCM) at a Numbered Fleet or component command
Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON), Pentagon

related_base_note: The Force Master Chief of U.S. Fleet Forces Command serves at Naval Station Norfolk.

faqs.question: What is MCPON?
faqs.answer: The Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy (MCPON) is the U.S. Navy's senior enlisted leader, serving as the senior enlisted advisor to the Chief of Naval Operations and to the Secretary of the Navy. The position was established in 1967 and is held by a single Master Chief at any given time.

faqs.question: What is the difference between CMC, FORCM, and FLTCM?
faqs.answer: All three are special billets at the E-9 paygrade. A Command Master Chief (CMC) advises a commanding officer at the unit level. A Force Master Chief (FORCM) advises at the Type Commander level. A Fleet Master Chief (FLTCM) advises at the Numbered Fleet or component-command level.
